questions.stem: In a compound interest investment, the interest for each period is calculated on:
options: the regular deposits but not the principal
the principal plus all interest already added
the original principal only, every period
the interest from the previous period only
questions.explanation: Compound interest is added to the balance, so later interest is earned on earlier interest as well as on the principal. Interest on the original principal only is simple interest, which grows linearly.

questions.stem: A future-value annuity is an investment in which:
options: a single deposit earns simple interest every year
interest is paid out each period and never reinvested
equal regular deposits are made and earn compound interest
a lump sum is drawn down by equal regular withdrawals
questions.explanation: A future-value annuity builds up savings: equal deposits are made each period and the balance earns compound interest. A lump sum drawn down by regular withdrawals is a present-value annuity, used to provide an income.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a present-value annuity?
options: A term deposit that pays all its interest at maturity
A share portfolio that pays a dividend twice a year
A retirement lump sum that pays a fixed monthly income
A savings plan with a fixed deposit every month
questions.explanation: A present-value annuity starts with a lump sum that is reduced by regular payments to the investor, like a superannuation pension. A savings plan with regular deposits is a future-value annuity, the reverse process.

questions.stem: The effective annual rate of an investment is:
options: the nominal rate divided by the number of compounding periods
the interest rate left after income tax has been deducted
the rate the institution charges each year as an account fee
the rate that, compounded yearly, gives the same yearly return
questions.explanation: The effective annual rate converts any compounding pattern to one compounding a year, so investments with different structures can be compared on a common basis. Dividing the nominal rate by the number of periods gives the rate per period, not an annual rate.

questions.stem: In Australia, interest earned on a savings account is:
options: taxed only if it is withdrawn from the account
part of taxable income for the year it is earned
free of tax because it is not earned by working
taxed only in the year the account is closed
questions.explanation: Interest is income, so it is added to taxable income for the year and taxed at the person's marginal rate. Leaving it in the account does not avoid the tax, which is why tax reduces the real return on savings.

questions.stem: Savings earn 3% p.a. after tax while inflation runs at 4% p.a. What happens to the savings?
options: Their purchasing power falls each year
They still grow in real terms each year
Their dollar balance falls each year
Their interest rate rises to match inflation
questions.explanation: Prices are rising faster than the balance, so each year the savings buy less even though the dollar balance keeps growing. Real growth needs the after-tax return to exceed the inflation rate.

questions.stem: At the same nominal rate, changing from yearly to monthly compounding makes the future value of a lump sum:
options: smaller, because each period's rate is twelve times less
the same, because the nominal annual rate is unchanged
twelve times larger, as there are twelve times the periods
larger, because interest starts earning interest sooner
questions.explanation: With monthly compounding, each month's interest is added and starts earning interest straight away, so the effective annual rate is higher. The smaller rate per period is exactly offset by more periods, and the compounding on top gives a little more.

questions.stem: For a future-value annuity, the total interest earned equals:
options: the regular deposit multiplied by the interest rate
the future value divided by the number of deposits
the future value minus the total of all the deposits
the future value minus the final deposit only
questions.explanation: Everything in the account at the end is either money deposited or interest, so interest = future value − (deposit × number of deposits). Subtracting only the last deposit ignores all the money put in earlier.

questions.stem: Superannuation is best described as:
options: money saved over a working life to fund retirement
a government payment made to every retired person
a loan taken out against the value of a home
a short-term account for saving towards a holiday
questions.explanation: Superannuation is a long-term savings scheme: contributions made during a working life are invested, and the balance later provides income in retirement, often as an annuity. A government payment to retirees is a pension, not superannuation.

questions.stem: Why might the result of a 30-year savings annuity calculation be unreliable?
options: Compound interest stops growing after twenty years
Deposits cannot be made more often than yearly
Interest rates are unlikely to stay fixed for 30 years
The formula is valid only for terms under ten years
questions.explanation: The annuity model assumes the same interest rate and deposit for the whole term. Over decades rates change, and fees, tax and inflation also affect the outcome, so the result is an estimate, not a guarantee.

questions.stem: A savings plan has a fixed monthly account-keeping fee taken from the balance. Compared with the same plan without the fee, the final balance is:
options: lower by exactly the total of the fees
lower by less than the total of the fees
the same, as the fee is charged separately
lower by more than the total of the fees
questions.explanation: Each fee removes money that would have earned compound interest for the rest of the term, so the loss is the fees plus the interest they would have earned. Only if no interest were paid would the loss equal the fees alone.

questions.stem: $8000 is invested at 4.8% p.a. compounded monthly for 5 years. What is the future value?
questions.explanation: The monthly rate is 0.048/12 = 0.004 and there are 60 months, so FV = 8000 × 1.004^60 = $10 165.13. $10 113.38 compounds yearly, and $9920.00 is simple interest.

questions.stem: How much must be invested now at 6% p.a. compounded quarterly to have $20 000 in 4 years?
questions.explanation: The quarterly rate is 1.5% and there are 16 quarters, so PV = 20 000 / 1.015^16 = $15 760.62. $18 843.68 uses only 4 periods, treating years as quarters.

questions.stem: $5000 is invested at 5.4% p.a. compounded monthly. What is the least number of whole months needed for it to reach $7000?
options: 89 months
84 months
75 months
74 months
questions.explanation: Solving 5000 × 1.0045^n = 7000 gives n = 74.94, so 75 whole months are needed; after 74 months the balance is just under $7000. 89 months is the simple interest answer, which ignores interest on interest.

questions.stem: $10 000 grows to $12 000 in 4 years with interest compounded yearly. What is the annual interest rate, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: Solving 10 000 × (1 + i)^4 = 12 000 gives (1 + i) = 1.2^(1/4), so i = 4.66%. 5% is the simple interest rate, 2000/10 000/4, which is too high because compounding adds interest on interest.

questions.stem: At 6% p.a. compounded monthly, what is the least number of whole months for an investment to double?
options: 144 months
139 months
200 months
138 months
questions.explanation: Solving 1.005^n = 2 gives n = 138.98, so 139 months (11 years 7 months); after 138 months it is just short of double. 200 months is the simple interest time, 1/0.06 years.

questions.stem: $200 is deposited at the end of every month for 10 years into an account paying 6% p.a. compounded monthly. What is the future value?
questions.explanation: Here i = 0.005 and n = 120, so FV = 200 × (1.005^120 − 1)/0.005 = $32 775.87. $24 000.00 is just the deposits, and $32 939.75 would apply if deposits were made at the start of each month.

questions.stem: $200 is deposited at the end of every month for 10 years into an account paying 6% p.a. compounded monthly. How much interest is earned?
questions.explanation: The future value is $32 775.87 and the deposits total 200 × 120 = $24 000, so the interest is $8775.87. $14 400 is simple interest on $24 000 for 10 years, which overstates it because most deposits are made well after the start.

questions.stem: A plan has deposits of $200 at the end of each month for 10 years at 6% p.a. compounded monthly. Which values of n and i are used?
questions.explanation: With monthly deposits and monthly compounding, n counts months (12 × 10 = 120) and i is the monthly rate (0.06/12 = 0.005). Mixing a yearly rate with monthly periods is a common slip.

questions.stem: What quarterly deposit, made at the end of each quarter, will grow to $50 000 in 8 years at 4.4% p.a. compounded quarterly?
questions.explanation: Here i = 0.011 and n = 32, so the deposit is 50 000 × 0.011/(1.011^32 − 1) = $1312.09. $1562.50 is 50 000/32, which ignores the interest the deposits earn.

questions.stem: Mia deposits $500 at the end of each month at 4.2% p.a. compounded monthly. How many deposits does she need to make for the balance to reach at least $40 000?
options: 67 deposits
71 deposits
80 deposits
70 deposits
questions.explanation: Solving 500 × (1.0035^n − 1)/0.0035 = 40 000 gives n = 70.65, so 71 deposits are needed; after 70 the balance is just short. 80 deposits ignores interest altogether.

questions.stem: A ten-year plan has $250 deposited at the end of each month at 5.4% p.a. compounded monthly. What is the balance after the first 3 years?
questions.explanation: After 36 deposits with i = 0.0045, the balance is 250 × (1.0045^36 − 1)/0.0045 = $9746.28. $39 662.74 is the balance at the end of the full ten years.

questions.stem: An account opens with $5000, and $100 is added at the end of every month for 5 years at 6% p.a. compounded monthly. What is the final balance?
questions.explanation: The opening $5000 grows to 5000 × 1.005^60 = $6744.25 and the deposits grow to 100 × (1.005^60 − 1)/0.005 = $6977.00, a total of $13 721.25. Adding $5000 without interest forgets that the opening balance also compounds.

questions.stem: Liam earns $1250 interest in a year and pays tax at 30 cents in the dollar on it. How much interest does he keep?
questions.explanation: The tax is 0.30 × 1250 = $375, so he keeps 1250 − 375 = $875.00. Dividing by 1.3 treats the tax as if it were added on top rather than taken out.

questions.stem: With inflation of 2.5% p.a., what is $25 000 in 10 years' time worth in today's dollars?
questions.explanation: Inflation acts like compound interest on prices, so the present value is 25 000 / 1.025^10 = $19 529.96. $18 750.00 subtracts 2.5% of $25 000 ten times, treating inflation as simple.

questions.stem: $10 000 is invested for one year at 5% p.a. compounded yearly. Tax of 30% is paid on the interest, and inflation for the year is 3%. Has real growth occurred?
options: No, tax and inflation together take away 33%
Yes, the full $10 500 is well above $10 300
Yes, $10 350 after tax beats the $10 300 needed
No, $10 350 after tax is below the $10 500 needed
questions.explanation: Interest is $500, tax is $150, so $10 350 remains. Keeping pace with 3% inflation needs $10 300, so there is a small real gain of $50. Ignoring the tax overstates the gain, and adding 30% and 3% as rates makes no sense.

questions.stem: Ella deposits $300 at the end of each month for 5 years at 4.8% p.a. compounded monthly, but a $5 fee is taken out of each deposit. By how much does the fee reduce her final balance?
questions.explanation: Each deposit is effectively $295, so the loss is the future value of $5 a month: 5 × (1.004^60 − 1)/0.004 = $338.30. $300 is just the fees themselves, which ignores the interest they would have earned.

questions.stem: Two accounts pay the same interest rate. Account P charges a $4 monthly fee and Account Q charges a $40 yearly fee. Over a year, which is cheaper?
options: They cost the same over a full year
P, since its fee is charged in smaller amounts
Q, since $40 a year is less than $48 a year
P, since $4 a month is the smaller charge
questions.explanation: Twelve monthly fees of $4 total $48, which is more than the $40 yearly fee. Comparing $4 with $40 directly ignores how often each fee is charged.

questions.stem: What is the effective annual rate of 6% p.a. compounded monthly?
questions.explanation: The effective rate is (1 + 0.06/12)^12 − 1 = 1.005^12 − 1 = 6.17%. 6.14% is the result for quarterly compounding, which is a little lower than monthly.

questions.stem: Account A pays 5.2% p.a. compounded monthly. Account B pays 5.3% p.a. compounded yearly. Which pays more, and why?
options: B, as its nominal rate is 0.1% higher
A, as its effective rate is 5.30% p.a.
B, as yearly compounding adds more each time
A, as its effective rate is 5.33% p.a.
questions.explanation: A's effective rate is (1 + 0.052/12)^12 − 1 = 5.33%, which beats B's 5.30% (yearly compounding means B's effective rate equals its nominal rate). 5.30% would be A's rate with quarterly compounding.

questions.stem: A 3-year bond pays 6% p.a. flat (simple) interest, all at maturity. What equivalent effective annual rate, compounded yearly, gives the same return?
questions.explanation: Flat interest of 6% for 3 years returns 18% in total, so (1 + i)^3 = 1.18 and i = 5.67%. The equivalent compound rate is lower than 6% because compounding earns interest on interest.

questions.stem: $10 000 is invested for 5 years. Which earns more: 5.5% p.a. simple interest or 5% p.a. compounded yearly?
options: Simple, as 5.5% is the higher of the two rates
They earn exactly the same amount
Compound, $2762.82 against $2750
Simple, $2750 against $2500.00
questions.explanation: Simple interest is 10 000 × 0.055 × 5 = $2750. Compound interest is 10 000 × 1.05^5 − 10 000 = $2762.82, slightly more. $2500 is simple interest at 5%, which is not the compound offer.

questions.stem: A $400 000 superannuation lump sum is invested at 4.8% p.a. compounded monthly to pay a monthly income for 20 years, leaving nothing at the end. What is the monthly payment?
questions.explanation: This is a present-value annuity with i = 0.004 and n = 240: payment = 400 000 × 0.004/(1 − 1.004^−240) = $2595.83. $1600 is the interest alone each month, which would keep the lump sum intact forever.

questions.stem: $300 000 is invested at 4.2% p.a. compounded monthly, and $2500 is withdrawn at the end of each month. For how many months can the full $2500 be withdrawn?
options: 120 months
156 months
179 months
155 months
questions.explanation: Solving 300 000 = 2500 × (1 − 1.0035^−n)/0.0035 gives n = 155.91, so 155 full withdrawals, with a smaller final one. 120 months ignores the interest earned while the money is being drawn down.

questions.stem: What lump sum, invested at 4.8% p.a. compounded monthly, will provide $3000 at the end of each month for 25 years?
questions.explanation: The lump sum is the present value: 3000 × (1 − 1.004^−300)/0.004 = $523 562.99. $900 000 is the total paid out, which ignores the interest earned while the balance runs down.

questions.stem: A retiree's lump sum earns interest at exactly the same amount as her monthly withdrawal. What happens to the balance?
options: It halves after the first twelve months
It stays the same and lasts indefinitely
It slowly falls and runs out eventually
It slowly rises by the interest each month
questions.explanation: Each month the interest added equals the money taken out, so the balance never changes, like a perpetuity. Withdrawing more than the interest makes the balance fall and eventually run out.

questions.stem: A retiree has a fixed lump sum to fund a monthly income. Which change would allow a larger monthly payment?
options: Paying an extra yearly management fee
Taking the income over a shorter period
Taking the income over a longer period
Investing at a lower rate of interest
questions.explanation: A shorter period spreads the same lump sum over fewer payments, so each one can be larger. A longer period, a lower rate or extra fees all reduce the payment the lump sum can support.

questions.stem: Doubling the monthly deposit in a future-value annuity, with the same rate and term, makes the future value:
options: exactly double
more than double
less than double
four times as large
questions.explanation: The future value is the deposit multiplied by ((1 + i)^n − 1)/i, which does not depend on the deposit, so doubling the deposit doubles the future value. Doubling the term, by contrast, more than doubles it.

questions.stem: Two people each deposit $100 a month at the same rate. Ana deposits for the first 10 years only and leaves the money invested. Ben deposits for the next 10 years only. After 20 years, who has more?
options: They have the same, as each deposited $12 000
Ben, as a later start means a higher balance
Ana, as her deposits earn interest for longer
Ben, as his deposits are made more recently
questions.explanation: Both deposit $12 000, but Ana's money earns compound interest for the whole 20 years, while Ben's has at most 10 years to grow. Starting to save early matters more than the timing of the same total deposits.
